Upon entering the theater, you're greeted by ushers in period garb who regale you with comic banter and musical numbers. This immersion continues with the show proper, which ingeniously incorporates old-style film images and projections into which the characters pop in and out.

Last winter, fortunate theatergoers fell madly, hopelessly in love with 'Brief Encounter,' the enchanting British spin on the Noel Coward movie that had a limited sold-out run at the adventurous little St. Ann's Warehouse under the Brooklyn Bridge. As it turns out, our brief affair was not hopeless after all.
The acrobatics of love are performed in high style in “Brief Encounter,” which is surely the most enchanting work of stagecraft ever inspired by a movie.

Work as imaginative and wholly successful as "Brief Encounter" doesn't come along every day.
In 1945, master imp and conscientious keeper-of-British-values Noel Coward adapted his one-act Still Life into Brief Encounter, the seminal stiff-upper-lip-tearjerker film now beloved by millions.

Even if you're not familiar with David Lean's 1946 movie melodrama Brief Encounter, you will find yourself caught up in writer-director Emma Rice's brilliantly reconceived stage adaptation, now playing at Broadway's Studio 54 following a successful run last winter at Brooklyn's St. Ann's Warehouse. (EW's original review).
Emma Rice’s 90 minute encounter with Noel Coward’s great work -- equally sublime -- stands on its own.

Proving once more that Noel Coward wrote sexier scenes for clothed people that most playwrights could with naked ones, the evening's steamy highlight comes in a moment where Yelland and Sturrock, alone together at last, finally reach the "will we or won't we" point.
But what's missing is the movie's emotional core the impassioned delicacy of its portrayal of two people who glimpse all too briefly the romance that their ordinary lives can never permit.
The result is a hash that neither honors the original nor justifies spoofing it at such length.
If you want to have a very good time, go to this production.

cn.t: Critics mostly embrace this inventive British import for its enchanting stagecraft and playful multimedia storytelling, though some find Rice's flashy approach overwhelms Coward's emotional restraint.

sg.ra: SeatPlan names Center Orchestra rows E-G as the best seats overall, citing 'a winning mix of perfect proximity and elevated view over the heads in front' on a good rake with a low stage. Headout notes the 'outstanding inclination' keeps sightlines clear from middle rows. AVFMS Row D seat 2: 'Perfect view with unlimited legroom.' 16-row section seats ~350 of the 413 total; low stage means front rows don't require neck strain.

SeatPlan explicitly names Left and Right Mezzanine as 'the best value seats at the Laura Pels Theatre,' citing cheap tickets vs. central Orchestra with 'a clear and close view.' Only 3 rows (AA/BB/CC), under 100 seats — feels intimate and close to stage. Headout confirms 'very little restriction from the Mezzanine overhang at the back' of the Orchestra, meaning the Mezzanine itself is close/low. Row BB flagged by Headout as a specific value row.
